newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Confusion as weary Mobutu returns home to Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Confusion as weary Mobutu returns home to Zaire.

text.p: Zaire's ailing and embattled President Mobutu Sese Seko returned home on Friday to try to salvage what remains of his crumbling authority in the face of relentless rebel advances, witnesses said.

But his homecoming created considerable confusion about his state of health after aides from his plane and his presidential guard ushered away a welcoming committee of senior military men and government ministers.
"I think he was tired and did not want to be seen being helped down the aircraft steps," a senior government official told Reuters later.
An aide to Mobutu, who has just had fresh cancer treatment, said the veteran president's wife Bobila Dawa had helped him down the steps before they travelled to his official residence.

Mobutu's low-key return contrasted with his December 17 homecoming, when large crowds turned out to welcome him. On Friday small crowds gathered on the airport route in opposition areas to jeer Mobutu and praise rebel leader Laurent Kabila.
Kabila, meanwhile, arrived in triumph in Zaire's third city of Kisangani on Friday, where more than 10,000 jubilant residents hailed him as a saviour.
Kabila, whose forces have been fighting to topple Mobutu since October and captured Kisangani last week, rejected a truce-then-talks call from Mobutu. "We negotiate first," Kabila said in Kisangani.
"He (Mobutu) always wants to buy time. But we will not play his game," his political commissioner Deo Bugera added.
Mobutu, 66, left hospital in Monaco on Wednesday after fresh cancer treatment. He issued a statement on Thursday calling for a truce and a national council to find a peace settlement.
"He will address the nation to mark his position clearly," his son Mobutu Nzanga told Reuters in Nice. "My father remains an important player in the stability of Central Africa."

But many ordinary Zaireans, eager for a change from three decades of poverty and hardship under Mobutu, are openly rallying to Kabila. Residents of Kinshasa's poor districts openly welcome the prospect of his arrival in the capital.
Meanwhile, U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen said that U.S. officials were monitoring the rebellion in Zaire day by day, even hour by hour, to assess whether to evacuate U.S. citizens.
"We are in the preparatorial stage to make sure we can act if action is called for," Cohen told reporters in Washington.

Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL) is advancing relentlessly across the sprawling and chaotic Central African nation, where central government control has long been notional in many places.
Under foreign pressure to agree a truce and talk, Kabila says only face-to-face talks with Mobutu can halt the fighting.

Mobutu's son Nzanga said on Thursday that his father no longer ruled out talks with rebel leaders but wanted to involve the government, army and transitional parliament. "His intention is to find a solution to the present crisis in consultation with parliament, the government and the military high command."

Mobutu has spent most of his time in Europe since having prostate cancer surgery in August. He has dominated Zaire with a mixture of political acumen and military ruthlessness since seizing power in 1965.
He presented his proposed national council as a formula to find "appropriate ways" out of the crisis "with all our brothers, without exclusion".

The rebels were not the only ones unimpressed. "He is sure to come with his usual confusion. Everything is possible, a good move, a bad move and the worst possible move. But he will above all be thinking of himself," one senior government member said.

The rebels took up arms in October in a dispute about Zairean nationality for an ethnic Tutsi minority, who form the core of Kabila's fighting force. An alliance of anti-Mobutu groups rallied around the cause.
